Shares of Rocket Lab (RKLB) rebounded after a six-session losing streak on Tuesday as CEO Peter Beck highlighted the company as one of the few proven commercial launch providers, calling SpaceX a “friendly rival” and noting that Rocket Lab emerged from a field of more than 100 failed challengers. RKLB stock jumped nearly 3% on Tuesday, with shares also up nearly 2% overnight. In a recent BBC interview, Beck said commercial launch remains exceptionally difficult despite billions of dollars in investment. “Despite billions of dollars and over 100 companies trying, there has actually only been two companies to pop out the other end,” with a regular and reliable launch service, he said, in a discussion that also touched on Rocket Lab’s rivalry with SpaceX. “Launch and a commercial company doing launch still remains extremely rare,” Beck added. Beck called SpaceX a “friendly rival” and said space companies often compete for one contract before working together on another: “You can be competing tooth and tail for a particular contract” and later team up to deliver it, he said. Rocket Lab can also benefit when rivals win as it supplies components such as reaction wheels, star trackers and solar panels.” “We can go head to head with a traditional space prime and then lose,” Beck said. “And then the next day, there’s a purchase order.” Beck called Rocket Lab an end-to-end space company spanning satellites, launch and services from orbit: “We build satellites, we launch them on our rockets and we provide services from space,” he said. Pointing to SpaceX’s Falcon 9 and Starlink model, Beck added: “They’re able to do all those things. And we’re able to do those too.” William Blair analyst Louie DiPalma recently named Rocket Lab and Blue Origin among the strongest challengers to SpaceX, though he said SpaceX still holds more than 90% of the launch market. Rocket Lab is advancing its competitive vertical integration strategy through its $8 billion acquisition of Iridium Communications, which would add a global network, spectrum, and recurring satellite service revenue. The company recently completed a full-duration burn of its Archimedes Vacuum engine, an important step toward the first flight of its reusable Neutron rocket. Rocket Lab said it was “critical preparation for Neutron’s first flight.” Beck has told Stocktwits earlier that Rocket Lab is “pushing very hard” to launch Neutron by the fourth quarter of 2026, while cautioning that the challenge is not merely reaching orbit but proving the rocket can return and be reused. “If we just had to go up, it’s super easy, we’d be in orbit by now,” he previously said. Rocket Lab also completed the U.S. Space Force’s Victus Haze mission, launching 16 hours and 42 minutes after receiving notice and completing spacecraft commissioning and proximity operations ahead of schedule. The company supplied the launch vehicle, spacecraft and orbital operations under one contract, offering a practical demonstration of the integrated model Beck outlined in the interview. "While we anticipated some supply-chain related impact in our expectations, we did not anticipate ​the magnitude of the capex reprioritization," Krishna said, adding that the company “faltered” and "numerous large deals" had failed to close as expected. IBM said the weakness was largely in its mainframe business, which sells high-end enterprise computers and related software that power mission-critical workloads, including processing massive volumes of transactions for banks, governments, airlines, and retailers. It also noted that businesses were prioritizing cybersecurity due to recent advances in AI, including the release of Anthropic’s powerful Mythos technology. The bottom-line figures were rather concerning, with the gross profit margin expected to drop by 100 basis points to 57.7%. IBM shares dropped a record 25.2% on Tuesday. The comments intensified concerns about AI-driven disruption across the software industry, fears that have been building for months and weighing on software stocks. This is deliberate institutional ‘conflation’ not lazy analysis,” argued a trader. “There was less SAAS shorting and even some covering in the last couple of weeks but I'm pretty sure we will see that go up next several sessions until NOW reports next week. Could be an inflection point if positive.” For updates and corrections, email newsroom[at]stocktwits[dot]com. Comments posted here will also appear on symbol pages. General Fusion Group Ltd. (GFUZ) made history on Monday, becoming the first pure-play nuclear fusion energy company to trade on a major public stock exchange. In an exclusive interview with Stocktwits, CEO Greg Twinney argued that fusion is not just a cleaner alternative to fission but is a fundamentally larger market opportunity. GFUZ stock surged 21% on its debut, added over 25% on Tuesday, and was trading about 2.5% lower in the overnight session. The Vancouver-based company, backed by Amazon founder Jeff Bezos, among others, went public through a SPAC merger with Spring Valley Acquisition Corp. III, which provided General Fusion with approximately $150 million in cash. Earlier, Twinney told the Wall Street Journal that the funding is sufficient to meet the scientific milestones required by its demonstration machine. The listing arrives at a pivotal moment. Surging electricity demand driven by the AI boom, the global spread of electrification, and the energy appetite of large-scale computing has renewed urgency around new sources of firm, clean power. Fusion has attracted growing investment and government attention as a potential long-term answer. According to the Financial Times, the number of private fusion companies has more than doubled over the past five years, intensifying competition at a time when the technology is still roughly a decade from commercialization. General Fusion is targeting its first commercial plant around 2035. Twinney's bull case for fusion starts with what it doesn't produce. Unlike fission, fusion does not generate long-lived radioactive waste, does not use fuels that could be weaponized, and carries no risk of a meltdown. "Fusion is just inherently safe. We're not needing to engineer safety into it in the same way that you need to with fission," he told Stocktwits. "When fusion fails, it kind of just fails safely and there's not really any fallout from that." That safety profile has a direct commercial implication: regulators around the world are moving to govern fusion "in a much lighter way" than conventional nuclear, Twinney said, which he believes creates the potential to site fusion plants closer to population centers and industrial demand. That's a significant advantage over fission, which requires remote, heavily secured facilities. "We get all the benefits that fission can provide without the downsides," he said. There's another significant advantage. Fusion reactors primarily use deuterium, which can be extracted from seawater and is "massively abundant." The other component, tritium, is rarer in nature but can be bred through the interaction of a neutron and lithium. Fission, by contrast, relies on uranium and other finite sources. "The overall market size because of the safety profile and the abundance of fuel in fusion is much bigger than fission," Twinney said. While advanced nuclear companies such as Oklo Inc. (OKLO) and NuScale Power Corp. (SMR) are often thought of as being closer to commercialization than fusion technology, Twinney said that the gap may not be as large as investors assume. While the road to commercialization for fusion technology has its challenges, including achieving reactor durability, tritium fuel breeding, economic viability, and the ability to efficiently extract and convert fusion energy into electricity, he argues small modular reactor (SMR) timelines also struggle with regulatory hurdles that can make timelines less predictable than they appear today. "I know that the timelines for SMRs, which can be very unpredictable due to regulations and those types of things, [are] probably not that different," he said. According to Twinney, the combination of abundant fuel supplies and a lighter regulatory framework could ultimately enable fusion to scale faster than conventional nuclear technologies once commercial viability has been demonstrated. However, Twinney does not view fusion and fission as mutually exclusive technologies. "They will be complementing each other," he said. "And I think that fusion kind of rounds out the nuclear circle if you think about it that way," he added. When asked about criticism from former Commonwealth Fusion Systems CTO Dan Brunner, who, in a recent interview with the Financial Times, said General Fusion's commercialization timeline was "very hard to believe," Twinney said the company’s timelines were based on real experimental results from its Lawson Machine 26. The machine is designed to demonstrate that plasma can be heated through mechanical compression rather than superconducting magnets or high-powered lasers, he said, adding that the company's early results validated the operating principles behind its MTF approach that are “not based on fiction or papers being written.” The timelines “are based on our real results from machines that we have built and operated and then eventually written papers on. But those are real results papers, not theoretical papers,” he said. Twinney also emphasized that General Fusion's approach could offer a cost advantage over many competing technologies. While many other fusion developers rely on expensive superconducting magnets, high-powered lasers, or advanced materials that have yet to be proven at commercial scale, General Fusion's Magnetized Target Fusion (MTF) system uses mechanical compression and a liquid-lithium wall that can protect reactor components from neutron damage, help with breeding tritium fuel, and absorbing fusion energy as heat that can be converted into electricity using conventional steam turbines. In an earlier interview with Stocktwits, Chief Strategy Officer Megan Wilson had also pointed to the economic advantages of MTF, which eliminate the need for expensive magnets, targets, lasers, or exotic, not-yet-invented materials. The technology also eliminates the need for frequent replacement of components damaged by neutron exposure, she had said. “Our plants are designed to be cost-competitive compared to coal, steam, and natural gas,” she had said then. “They are expected to deliver four times as much energy per unit of fuel as fission, without long-lived radioactive waste, positioning them as the superior nuclear technology for sustainable growth.” By avoiding costly magnets and lasers and using existing industrial technologies, Twinney said he believes General Fusion has a clearer path to building an economically viable power plant, as the company’s design has from the beginning aimed to avoid the major barriers to commercializing fusion. "What we are trying to do at General Fusion, and our power plant design from the beginning, has been we want to avoid the major barriers to commercializing fusion. Not just demonstrate a bunch of fusion, but actually avoid the barriers to commercializing it," he said. On Stocktwits, retail sentiment around GFUZ stock is ‘bullish’ amid ‘high’ message volumes. The contrast between broader market weakness and relative stability across major banking names made the session especially notable, with the  S&P 500 providing an important backdrop for the broader equity mood. The banking sector entered the latest session with several forces working at once. Long-term Treasury yields remained elevated, while fresh economic commentary kept expectations around monetary policy in motion. At the same time, geopolitical developments near an important global shipping corridor added uncertainty to energy markets and the wider economy. For JPMorgan Chase, those developments matter because the company operates across numerous financial channels. Its consumer banking business connects it to household activity, while commercial and corporate lending provides exposure to business demand. Its markets operations can benefit from periods of heightened trading activity, while wealth and asset management provide recurring fee-based revenue. That combination makes JPMorgan Chase more than a conventional lender. The company serves as a broad financial intermediary whose performance can reflect changes in interest rates, credit conditions, market activity, consumer behavior, and corporate demand. Long-term Treasury yields influence the economics of banking because they affect the pricing of loans, securities, and other financial stock assets. When market rates remain firm, newly originated loans can carry higher yields, while the cost of deposits and other funding sources also becomes an important consideration. The relationship is not straightforward. Banks must balance the revenue generated from interest-earning assets against the cost of funding those assets. Deposit behavior therefore becomes especially important when rates remain elevated. For a diversified institution such as JPMorgan Chase, the effect is spread across a large balance sheet. Consumer loans, commercial facilities, mortgages, cards, and securities can each respond differently to changes in the rate environment. This diversification can reduce reliance on any single part of the banking model. It also gives the market several different indicators to monitor when assessing how a firm is navigating the rate cycle. Federal Reserve commentary added another layer to the banking discussion. Remarks describing the U.S. economy through the lens of secular growth encouraged attention toward the durability of economic activity, while uncertainty surrounding inflation continued to influence expectations around monetary policy. For banks, economic growth and interest rates are closely connected. Stronger economic activity can support credit demand, business expansion, household spending, and financial-market activity. However, persistent inflation can make monetary policymakers more cautious about easing financial conditions. That tension creates a complicated backdrop for lenders. Banks can benefit from healthy economic activity, but elevated borrowing costs can also influence household affordability and corporate financing decisions. JPMorgan Chase's broad customer base gives it exposure to both sides of that equation. The company serves households and businesses while also operating major financial-market and wealth-management platforms. Diversification remains one of JPMorgan Chase's defining characteristics. The company operates across consumer and community banking, commercial banking, investment banking, markets, securities services, and wealth management. Each business responds differently to economic conditions. Consumer banking is influenced by spending, deposits, cards, mortgages, and household credit. Commercial banking responds to corporate financing needs and business investment. Markets operations can become more active when volatility rises, while wealth management depends heavily on client assets, financial activity, and recurring relationships. That breadth provides a wider operating base than a bank focused primarily on traditional lending. During uncertain sessions, the market therefore tends to examine the combined performance of these businesses rather than focusing solely on net interest margins. Geopolitical tension near the Strait of Hormuz contributed to concerns around energy markets and global supply routes. Such developments can affect financial markets well beyond crude prices. Periods of uncertainty often create greater demand for hedging, currency management, rates trading, commodities exposure, and other financial services. Large financial institutions with extensive market operations are positioned to intermediate those flows. JPMorgan Chase has a substantial presence across global financial markets, connecting institutional clients with a wide range of products and services. That does not mean volatility automatically translates into stronger financial results. Market swings can create both opportunities and risks. Still, a broad trading and markets franchise gives a major bank another source of activity when economic uncertainty increases. The consumer business remains an important part of the broader JPMorgan Chase story. Household spending, credit-card activity, deposits, mortgages, and other financial services provide insight into the condition of consumers. A growing economy can support transaction activity and credit demand, while elevated interest rates can increase the cost of borrowing. Credit quality becomes another critical consideration. Banks monitor whether households and businesses are keeping pace with their financial obligations, particularly when borrowing costs remain firm. Because JPMorgan Chase has extensive exposure to households, developments in consumer credit can provide an important signal about the health of the broader economy. Deposits are a central source of bank funding. The behavior of customers becomes especially important when interest rates remain elevated because depositors have more incentive to consider alternative places for their cash. The balance between interest-bearing and non-interest-bearing deposits can influence funding costs. A strong primary banking relationship can also provide stability because customers often maintain deposits for convenience, payments, lending relationships, and other services. JPMorgan Chase's large deposit franchise gives it significant scale in this area. As rates evolve, the relationship between deposit costs and asset yields remains an important factor in determining how the traditional banking operation performs. Commercial and corporate banking connects JPMorgan Chase with businesses across a broad range of industries. Companies use banks for credit facilities, treasury services, investment banking, payments, and capital-market activity. Economic growth can encourage businesses to expand operations, invest in infrastructure, manage inventories, and pursue strategic opportunities. Those activities can create demand for financial services. At the same time, elevated borrowing costs can make corporate financing decisions more selective. The diversified nature of JPMorgan Chase's commercial franchise means the company can observe business activity across numerous industries rather than relying on a narrow customer base. Wealth and asset management provide an important source of fee-based activity. Unlike traditional lending revenue, these businesses are not driven primarily by the difference between asset yields and funding costs. Client assets, advisory relationships, custody services, and investment-management activity can create recurring revenue streams across different market conditions. That gives JPMorgan Chase another layer of diversification. When rate-sensitive banking income faces changing conditions, fee-based businesses can provide an additional operating engine. The result is a financial model that depends on a wide collection of customer relationships rather than a single revenue source. The company's position also places it within the broader Financial Stock landscape, where interest rates, credit quality, economic growth, capital requirements, and market activity all shape sentiment. A softer market session does not necessarily mean every sector will respond in the same way. That distinction was visible as geopolitical uncertainty weighed on broader market sentiment while banking-specific factors continued to shape the outlook for major lenders. The Strait of Hormuz remains an important global energy and shipping route, meaning developments in the region can have consequences far beyond the energy market. Higher energy costs can influence inflation expectations, corporate expenses, household budgets, and economic growth. For financial institutions, those effects can eventually filter through to credit demand and borrower quality. Large banks also have exposure to energy-related businesses and global companies operating across international markets. JPMorgan Chase's global reach therefore gives it exposure to both domestic and international economic developments. Its financial-market operations can also respond to changes in currency, commodities, rates, and cross-border capital flows. Technology has become central to the modern banking model. JPMorgan Chase has invested heavily in technology infrastructure as financial services become increasingly digital. Technology can improve customer access, streamline internal processes, strengthen risk management, and support increasingly sophisticated financial products. For a bank operating across consumer, commercial, markets, and wealth-management businesses, technology also helps connect different parts of the franchise. The next phase of the banking story will depend on several interconnected developments. Treasury yields remain important because they influence loan pricing, securities portfolios, deposit costs, and broader financial conditions. Inflation data will also remain relevant to expectations around monetary policy. If inflation proves persistent, the rate environment could remain restrictive for longer. If price pressures ease more convincingly, expectations around future policy could shift. Credit quality will remain another important measure. Investors will watch household finances, corporate borrowing, provisions, and delinquency trends for signs of stress or resilience. Treasury yields, monetary-policy expectations, credit conditions, and trading activity can create sector-specific dynamics even when geopolitical concerns pressure major benchmarks. title: JPMorgan Drops 'Bullish' Stance On US Stocks After Warsh's Hawkish Tone At Jackson Hole, Shifts To 'Tactically Cautious' - Stocktwits
content: JPMorgan Chase & Co.’s trading team has stepped back from its bullish posture on U.S. equities, shifting to a tactically cautious stance ahead of the Federal Reserve’s upcoming policy decision. The recalibration follows recent hawkish remarks by Federal Reserve Chairman Kevin Warsh, which prompted financial markets to price in an increased probability of interest-rate hikes before the end of the year. In a note to clients on Monday, accessed by Bloomberg, Andrew Tyler, head of U.S. market intelligence at JPMorgan, noted that while fundamental economic conditions and corporate earnings remain robust, short-term pressures are likely to cause stock indexes to move sideways rather than extend recent gains. Market sentiment shifted after Kevin Warsh’s Jackson Hole speech on Friday, which emphasized that inflation shows little sign of meaningfully cooling. Unlike past central bank leaders, Warsh has offered limited forward guidance regarding the magnitude and duration of potential rate increases. Tyler pointed out that if the central bank resumes raising borrowing costs, investors will face heightened uncertainty about the trajectory of monetary policy. Financial markets responded swiftly to the hawkish tone. The yield on the benchmark U.S. 10-year Treasury note climbed past 4.75% on Monday, hitting its highest level since January 2025. Meanwhile, interest-rate swap contracts signaled about a 70% probability that the Fed will implement a quarter-point rate increase next month, according to Bloomberg data. The CME FedWatch Tool on Monday indicated a 65.9% probability of a 25 basis point hike in the September rate-setting meeting, up from 57%. JPMorgan's tactical pivot comes as Wall Street enters September, traditionally the weakest calendar month for U.S. stock performance. Beyond monetary policy concerns, Tyler highlighted several near-term vulnerabilities for equity markets, including a cooling of momentum among high-valuation artificial intelligence stocks. Rising energy prices following recent military strikes between the U.S. and Iran and increased pressure on rate-sensitive utilities and defensive sectors. Despite these obstacles, broader market positioning remains largely balanced, and the S&P 500 Index was still on track to post an approximate 2.5% gain for August, while the Dow was set to end its fifth straight month in the green. Investors are now focused on incoming macroeconomic reports to gauge the Fed's next move. The upcoming monthly U.S. employment report, projected by economists to show an addition of 55,000 jobs in August, will serve as an initial indicator following July's unexpected contraction. "Equity bull markets tend to end with either a hiking cycle or a recession," Tyler wrote, reassuring investors that an economic contraction remains highly improbable in the near term. Nevertheless, he cautioned that the central bank’s forthcoming gathering has officially turned into a "live meeting."
